cases.title: TypeScript All Request Vectors
cases.objective: TypeScript encodes all nine canonical mutation requests and matches every frozen fixture byte string and SHA-256 identity.
minimumAssertions: All nine operation names appear once in canonical order.
Every emitted request byte string and request hash equals the frozen vector.

cases.title: Python All Request Vectors
cases.objective: Python encodes all nine canonical mutation requests to byte-identical fixture vectors and SHA-256 identities.
minimumAssertions: All nine Python request encodings are present in canonical order.
Every Python byte string and hash exactly equals its TypeScript-independent frozen vector.

cases.title: Decode Encode Round Trip
cases.objective: Both runtimes decode and re-encode every canonical request without changing one byte or its identity hash.
minimumAssertions: Each runtime accepts all nine closed request shapes.
Decode followed by encode returns the exact original canonical bytes and hashes.

cases.title: Legal Boundary Request Sizes
cases.objective: Exact maximum identifiers, value carriers, and the 64-record append remain accepted within every declared bound.
minimumAssertions: Every exact upper-bound carrier is accepted by both native codecs.
The maximum append contains exactly 64 records and remains within canonical byte bounds.

cases.title: Exact Retry Request Identity
cases.objective: An exact operation retry after close and reopen matches stored request and result bytes without allocating a new sequence.
minimumAssertions: The retried result is byte-identical to the first committed result.
Ledger row count, maximum sequence, and singleton last sequence do not advance.

cases.title: Captured Before Authorization
cases.objective: Caller mutation before and after the authorization await cannot alter the detached canonical request stored by the provider.
minimumAssertions: The provider captures a detached request before invoking authorization.
Mutating every caller-owned carrier around the await leaves stored request bytes unchanged.

cases.title: Invalid Request UTF-8
cases.objective: A malformed UTF-8 request BLOB is rejected as corruption without disclosing hostile payload bytes.
minimumAssertions: Semantic audit rejects the first invalid UTF-8 byte sequence.
Records, ledger, sequence singleton, and transaction state remain unchanged.

cases.title: Noncanonical Request JSON
cases.objective: Valid JSON with noncanonical key order, escaping, or insignificant syntax is rejected by exact byte round-trip validation.
minimumAssertions: Decoded content equivalence cannot excuse byte-level noncanonical JSON.
Audit rejects each order and escaping mutation without repairing the database.

cases.title: Request Shape Drift
cases.objective: Missing required fields and unknown fields are rejected under the closed operation-specific request codec.
minimumAssertions: Every operation codec rejects a representative missing required field.
Every operation codec rejects an unknown field and persists no normalized substitute.

cases.title: Request Number Domain
cases.objective: Floats, unsafe integers, negative bounded values, and forbidden numeric carriers fail closed in both runtimes.
minimumAssertions: Every forbidden numeric representative is rejected before replay.
No runtime-specific coercion changes the typed failure or durable state.

cases.title: Request Size and Depth Exhaustion
cases.objective: One-above byte, nesting-depth, and collection bounds fail before unbounded allocation or durable mutation.
minimumAssertions: Byte and collection excesses return the exact quota failure.
Forbidden nesting returns the exact invalid-argument failure under bounded parsing.

cases.title: Request Hash Only Drift
cases.objective: Changing request_hash while retaining the original request BLOB is detected as semantic corruption.
minimumAssertions: Audit recomputes the request hash from canonical stored bytes.
A one-nibble hash mutation fails without changing any other row.

cases.title: Coherent Request Hash Row Mismatch
cases.objective: A coherently changed request BLOB and hash are rejected when their decoded context differs from row tenant or operation identity.
minimumAssertions: Audit binds decoded tenant and operation context to primary-key columns.
A self-consistent hostile BLOB and hash cannot migrate identity between rows.

cases.title: Swapped Request BLOBs
cases.objective: Two same-operation ledger rows cannot exchange otherwise valid request BLOB and hash pairs.
minimumAssertions: Each request remains bound to its exact operation ID and row context.
Swapping both BLOB and matching hash between rows is detected during replay.

cases.title: Operation Name Request Confusion
cases.objective: Changing operation_name or decoding canonical request bytes under another operation codec fails closed.
minimumAssertions: The ledger operation name selects exactly one closed request codec.
Cross-operation request confusion is rejected before state projection.

cases.title: Request Error Leak
cases.objective: Hostile request content and leak sentinels never enter structured errors, logs, diagnostics, or serialized campaign reports.
minimumAssertions: Every serialized failure surface passes the complete leak-sentinel scan.
Raw request bytes, paths, SQL, and hostile values are absent from output.

cases.title: First Sequence Is One
cases.objective: The first new mutation stores global commit sequence one and advances the singleton last sequence to exactly one.
minimumAssertions: The first committed ledger row has commit_sequence equal to one.
Ledger count, maximum sequence, and singleton last sequence all equal one.

cases.title: All Operation Global Order
cases.objective: Every mutation operation across tenants shares one globally unique, gap-free, contiguous commit order.
minimumAssertions: All nine mutation operation names contribute to one global sequence.
Sequences are unique and equal the integer interval from one through the row count.

cases.title: Equal Timestamp Order
cases.objective: Mutations committed in the same provider millisecond remain deterministically ordered by global sequence.
minimumAssertions: At least two committed rows retain the same provider timestamp.
Replay order follows commit_sequence and never uses timestamp as a tie breaker.

cases.title: Retry Does Not Advance
cases.objective: Repeated exact retry before and after restart leaves sequence count, maximum, and singleton unchanged.
minimumAssertions: Every retry returns the originally stored canonical result.
No retry inserts a ledger row or advances the global sequence singleton.

cases.title: Failed Decision Creates No Gap
cases.objective: Conflict, stale fence, legal hold, and invalid request decisions allocate no ledger row and no sequence value.
minimumAssertions: Each rejection returns its exact code, operation, and retryability tuple.
Sequence count, maximum, singleton, and every protected state family remain unchanged.

cases.title: Busy Retry Uses One Sequence
cases.objective: A bounded whole-transaction SQLite BUSY retry eventually commits exactly one mutation and one global sequence.
minimumAssertions: The retry loop restarts the complete transaction only after the competing writer releases.
Successful completion persists one ledger row, one physical effect, and one sequence.

cases.title: Mixed Process Contiguous Sequences
cases.objective: Concurrent TypeScript and Python writers produce unique contiguous sequences in observed commit order.
minimumAssertions: At least one native process from each runtime commits against the same explicit database.
The final ledger has no duplicate, gap, or runtime-partitioned sequence range.

cases.title: Safe Last Sequence
cases.objective: A fixture staged at MAX_SAFE_INTEGER minus one may commit MAX_SAFE_INTEGER exactly and retain safe carriers.
minimumAssertions: The staged singleton and matching ledger inventory are valid before the final mutation.
The final commit stores exactly 9007199254740991 without rounding in either runtime.

cases.title: Zero Sequence
cases.objective: A format-2 operation-ledger row with commit sequence zero is rejected as semantic corruption.
minimumAssertions: The structural or semantic audit rejects sequence zero.
No audit path treats zero as a legacy or unsequenced format-2 row.

cases.title: Negative Sequence
cases.objective: A negative global sequence is rejected structurally or semantically without numeric coercion.
minimumAssertions: Both native SQLite carrier paths reject the same negative sequence.
The singleton and all valid rows remain byte-identical after rejection.

cases.title: Duplicate Sequence
cases.objective: A duplicate global sequence cannot bypass uniqueness enforcement, index verification, or semantic audit.
minimumAssertions: The hostile fixture attempts both constraint-level and post-constraint duplicate forms.
At least one mandatory layer rejects before a replay result is accepted.

cases.title: Sequence Gap
cases.objective: Ledger sequences one and three without sequence two fail exact global contiguity validation.
minimumAssertions: Audit compares count, minimum, maximum, and singleton continuity.
A coherent singleton value of three cannot hide the missing sequence.

cases.title: Reordered Sequence Effects
cases.objective: Swapping sequences on two individually valid rows fails ordered replay preconditions or result derivation.
minimumAssertions: Request, result, and row hashes remain internally canonical during the swap attack.
Replay detects that the new order cannot produce the retained physical state and results.

cases.title: Singleton Row Drift
cases.objective: A sequence singleton lower or higher than ledger count and maximum is rejected as corruption.
minimumAssertions: The lower-than-maximum singleton mutation fails.
The higher-than-maximum singleton mutation fails without allocating missing rows.

cases.title: Sequence Overflow
cases.objective: Allocation beyond MAX_SAFE_INTEGER returns quota exceeded before any durable state or sequence mutation.
minimumAssertions: Both runtimes reject the same staged overflow boundary without numeric rounding.
Ledger count, maximum, singleton, and target physical state remain unchanged.

cases.title: Post-Baseline Legacy Insertion
cases.objective: An additional format-1 ledger row inserted after the sealed baseline fails exact count, root, and legacy inventory binding.
minimumAssertions: The baseline binds the complete legacy operation inventory at publication.
A later canonical-looking legacy row cannot enter replay or change public state.

cases.title: Empty V1 Baseline
cases.objective: An empty v1 database upgrades with deterministic baseline metadata and global sequence zero.
minimumAssertions: The published baseline represents an exact empty physical projection.
No synthetic operation row is created and the sequence singleton remains zero.

cases.title: Golden V0 to V2 Migration
cases.objective: The immutable v0 golden fixture traverses both migration edges and preserves every public value exactly.
minimumAssertions: The v0 source identity is verified before either migration executes.
The final v2 baseline, ledger, sequence, and public projections match frozen expectations.

cases.title: Golden V1 to V2 Migration
cases.objective: A representative immutable v1 fixture produces the exact frozen baseline bytes, root, and sequence state.
minimumAssertions: Every expected baseline entry has exact ordinal, key, state bytes, and chained hash.
Header count, projection hash, final root, and legacy inventory match frozen values.

cases.title: Large Streamed Baseline
cases.objective: A 100000-record identity inventory is baselined and audited with bounded memory and fixed-size batch reads.
minimumAssertions: Instrumentation proves enumeration uses bounded batches rather than whole-table materialization.
Final entry count, projection hash, root, and public state reconcile exactly.

cases.title: No Legacy Operations
cases.objective: State families that have no legacy ledger rows still seed an exact replay baseline.
minimumAssertions: Records, checkpoints, leases, holds, migration state, and cursor tails are inventoried independently of legacy operations.
Replay begins from the sealed baseline without reconstructing nonexistent requests.

cases.title: All Legacy Result Shapes
cases.objective: The baseline retains canonical legacy results for all nine mutation operation names without claiming reconstructed requests.
minimumAssertions: Every legacy operation result decodes and re-encodes to canonical bytes.
Legacy rows are bound into the baseline inventory while request_blob remains absent by format contract.

cases.title: TypeScript Migrate Python Audit
cases.objective: Python accepts and independently audits the exact baseline bytes and root produced by TypeScript migration.
minimumAssertions: TypeScript alone performs the migration against an explicit fixture copy.
Python independently recomputes every identity and produces an exact report match.

cases.title: Python Migrate TypeScript Audit
cases.objective: TypeScript accepts and independently audits the exact baseline bytes and root produced by Python migration.
minimumAssertions: Python alone performs the migration against an explicit fixture copy.
TypeScript independently recomputes every identity and produces an exact report match.

cases.title: Baseline Header Root Drift
cases.objective: Changing the sealed baseline final root or projection hash fails semantic integrity validation.
minimumAssertions: A final-root-only mutation is rejected.
A projection-hash-only mutation is rejected without regenerating metadata.

cases.title: Baseline Entry BLOB Drift
cases.objective: Changing a baseline key or state BLOB while retaining its original hash fails canonical and hash validation.
minimumAssertions: Key BLOB mutation fails canonical decoding or identity binding.
State BLOB mutation fails its entry hash before projection acceptance.

cases.title: Baseline Order Drift
cases.objective: An ordinal gap, entry reorder, or previous-hash chain break fails baseline validation.
minimumAssertions: Every ordinal is exactly contiguous in canonical entry order.
Every previous hash and entry hash is recomputed through the final root.

cases.title: Baseline Entry Deletion
cases.objective: Deleting one baseline entry fails count, root, and retained physical projection reconciliation.
minimumAssertions: The header count and chain root cannot be repaired implicitly.
Even coherently rewritten metadata fails exact physical inventory reconciliation.

cases.title: Baseline Entry Insertion
cases.objective: A duplicate or extra baseline entry fails exact inventory, count, and root validation.
minimumAssertions: Duplicate canonical keys cannot appear at different ordinals.
A novel extra entry fails reconciliation even with a coherently recomputed chain.

cases.title: Legacy Operation Drift
cases.objective: Deleting, inserting, renaming, retiming, or changing a legacy result row fails sealed baseline binding.
minimumAssertions: Every legacy row identity and canonical result is represented in baseline metadata.
All five mutation classes fail even when surrounding physical state remains plausible.

cases.title: Malformed Source Rollback
cases.objective: A corrupt v0 or v1 source refuses migration while preserving original application ID, user version, schema, and bytes.
minimumAssertions: Both malformed source versions fail before candidate publication.
A byte comparison proves the original source and all version metadata remain unchanged.

cases.title: Killed Baseline Publication
cases.objective: Process death during enumeration or after entry staging leaves no accepted partial v2 database and retry completes exactly once.
minimumAssertions: Nonce-acknowledged barriers kill separately during enumeration and after staging.
Reopen rejects or rolls back partial publication, then deterministic retry publishes one complete baseline.

cases.title: Append Replay
cases.objective: The canonical append request reconstructs every record identity, stream head, appended count, and exact public result.
minimumAssertions: Replay validates the complete record chain and tenant-wide record identity set.
The independently derived result BLOB exactly equals the stored append result BLOB.

cases.title: Historical Append After Advance
cases.objective: An early append remains exactly replayable after later operations advance the authoritative stream tail.
minimumAssertions: Replay derives the early result at its original commit sequence.
Later tail advancement neither overwrites nor reinterprets the historical request and result.

cases.title: Save Checkpoint Replay
cases.objective: Replay reconstructs the exact checkpoint, revision allocation, current summary, and public save result.
minimumAssertions: The checkpoint bound record and canonical value identities are independently verified.
Current state and immutable revision history reconcile bidirectionally.

cases.title: Delete Present and Absent
cases.objective: Ordered replay independently derives both present-checkpoint deletion and absent-checkpoint no-op results.
minimumAssertions: A real delete validates expected value hash and allocates exactly one delete revision.
An absent delete returns false without allocating a revision or changing physical state.

cases.title: Acquire Lease Replay
cases.objective: Lease acquisition replay reconciles counters, used identity, expiry arithmetic, active state, and exact result.
minimumAssertions: Expected fence and non-reuse decisions are evaluated at the committed provider time.
Epoch, fence, used ID, expiry, and public lease bytes all match physical state.

cases.title: Renew Lease Replay
cases.objective: Lease renewal replay preserves acquisition identity while deriving one strictly extended safe expiry.
minimumAssertions: The request binding matches the exact active lease and unexpired committed-time state.
Only expiry and update time change; epoch, fence, holder, and lease ID remain exact.

cases.title: Release Lease Replay
cases.objective: Lease release replay clears active identity while retaining monotonic counters, used IDs, and exact inspection result.
minimumAssertions: The release request binds the exact live lease ID, holder, and fence.
Physical released state and derived inspection bytes reconcile without losing non-reuse history.

cases.title: Expired Takeover Replay
cases.objective: The committed provider time proves takeover eligibility and yields one monotonic lease epoch and fence transition.
minimumAssertions: The prior active lease is expired at the takeover commit time.
The new unique lease ID, epoch, fence, and result reconcile exactly across runtimes.

cases.title: Legal Hold Replay
cases.objective: Legal-hold replay derives idempotent place and release transitions plus the exact sorted governance result.
minimumAssertions: Repeated placement preserves the original placed time and creates no duplicate hold.
Release and final canonical ordering match the physical hold inventory exactly.

cases.title: Migration Lock Replay
cases.objective: Migration-lock acquire, takeover, and release replay with exact counters, used IDs, expiry, and null release result.
minimumAssertions: Source and target versions, expected fence, time, and lock-ID non-reuse are replayed.
Active and released physical states plus every public result byte reconcile exactly.

cases.title: All Nine Alternating History
cases.objective: One coherent ordered history contains every mutation operation and replays to one exact reconciled final state.
minimumAssertions: All nine mutation names occur at least once in global sequence order.
Every derived intermediate result and every final physical state family reconciles.

cases.title: Equal Final Hold Histories
cases.objective: Distinct place and release histories ending in the same hold set replay correctly and remain cryptographically distinguishable.
minimumAssertions: Both histories derive the same final governance inventory.
Their request sequences and operation roots remain different and individually verifiable.

cases.title: Checkpoint Delete Recreate History
cases.objective: Allowed checkpoint save, delete, and recreate transitions retain exact immutable revision chronology.
minimumAssertions: Each real transition allocates the exact next scope revision.
Current checkpoint revision points to its exact retained put revision after replay.

cases.title: Historical Lease Result Forgery
cases.objective: A coherently changed historical acquire, renew, or release result and hash fails even after a later takeover.
minimumAssertions: Replay derives each historical lease result at its original sequence.
Later valid state cannot conceal a forged earlier canonical result.

cases.title: Append Result Tail Forgery
cases.objective: A changed append tail and coherently recomputed result hash fail against the request-derived immutable tail.
minimumAssertions: Stored result bytes remain canonical during the attack.
Replay independently derives and byte-compares the correct final batch tail.

cases.title: Append Valid Other Tail
cases.objective: An append result hash that names another valid record or stream still fails exact request and stream binding.
minimumAssertions: The substituted hash resolves to a real immutable record elsewhere.
Replay rejects it because tenant, stream, sequence, and request-derived record identity differ.

cases.title: Append Count Forgery
cases.objective: A changed appended-record count and matching result hash fail against the exact request batch length.
minimumAssertions: The hostile result is canonically encoded and internally hashed.
Replay derives appendedRecords only from the validated stored request batch.

cases.title: Checkpoint Result Forgery
cases.objective: Another canonical checkpoint summary fails exact request, value, record-bound, and revision binding.
minimumAssertions: The substituted summary is independently valid for another checkpoint.
Replay rejects its scope, identity, revision, or value mismatch for this operation.

cases.title: Delete Result Forgery
cases.objective: Flipping the canonical deleted boolean and recomputing its result hash fails ordered checkpoint replay.
minimumAssertions: Replay determines presence from shadow checkpoint state before the operation.
The forged boolean cannot change revision allocation or physical reconciliation.

cases.title: Lease Result Forgery
cases.objective: Changed lease identity, holder, epoch, fence, or time plus a matching result hash fails deterministic replay.
minimumAssertions: Every public lease result field is independently derived from request and shadow state.
Each single-field and coherent multi-field mutation is rejected.

cases.title: Governance Result Forgery
cases.objective: A changed legal-hold inventory and coherent hash fail against the ordered shadow hold set.
minimumAssertions: Replay derives the sorted hold inventory after every place or release.
A plausible result from another sequence or stream cannot be substituted.

cases.title: Migration Result Forgery
cases.objective: Forged migration-lock result fields or a non-null release result fail exact replay and physical reconciliation.
minimumAssertions: Acquire and takeover results are derived from sequence-time lock state.
Release-migration-lock accepts only the exact canonical null result.

cases.title: Mutation Without Ledger
cases.objective: A physical append, checkpoint, lease, hold, or migration change absent from replay fails final-state reconciliation.
minimumAssertions: Each authoritative state family is compared bidirectionally with the replay projection.
An extra physical row or changed physical field is never ignored.

cases.title: Ledger Without Mutation
cases.objective: A canonical request and result row without its required physical effect fails final-state reconciliation.
minimumAssertions: Replay applies the request and derives the missing projected state.
The physical-state absence is reported as corruption without synthesizing or repairing rows.

cases.title: TypeScript All Families Python Continue
cases.objective: TypeScript creates every state and ledger family, then Python audits every byte and continues at the next sequence.
minimumAssertions: Python independently recomputes all baseline, request, result, sequence, and state roots.
Its next committed mutation uses exactly the prior global sequence plus one.

cases.title: Python All Families TypeScript Continue
cases.objective: Python creates every state and ledger family, then TypeScript audits every byte and continues at the next sequence.
minimumAssertions: TypeScript independently recomputes all portable identities.
Its next committed mutation is contiguous and remains Python-auditable.

cases.title: TypeScript Event Snapshot Python Append
cases.objective: A Python append gains one global sequence while an existing TypeScript event snapshot excludes it exactly.
minimumAssertions: The TypeScript cursor continues without skip or duplicate at its frozen tail.
Live state and replay include the Python append at the exact next sequence.

cases.title: Python Checkpoint Snapshot TypeScript Mutate
cases.objective: A Python checkpoint continuation has no skip or duplicate after TypeScript mutates the live checkpoint set.
minimumAssertions: The snapshot yields the exact original ordered checkpoint identities.
Replay and live state include the TypeScript save or delete at its global sequence.

cases.title: Mixed Empty Tail Race
cases.objective: Separate TypeScript and Python processes racing one empty tail yield one append winner and one global sequence.
minimumAssertions: Exactly one process commits and the other receives the exact typed tail conflict.
Records, ledger count, distinct sequence count, and singleton last sequence all equal one.

cases.title: Mixed Lease Takeover
cases.objective: One runtime takes over an expired lease and the other runtime's stale writer fails without allocating a sequence.
minimumAssertions: Takeover commits one monotonic epoch, fence, used ID, and sequence.
The stale mutation changes neither physical state nor sequence singleton.

cases.title: Python Backup TypeScript Restore
cases.objective: TypeScript restores a Python backup, replays baseline and sequences, then continues with exactly sequence N plus one.
minimumAssertions: Backup and manifest bind every v2 identity before restore publication.
Restored semantic root and next sequence remain exact after TypeScript continuation.

cases.title: TypeScript Backup Python Restore
cases.objective: Python restores a TypeScript backup, replays baseline and sequences, then continues with exactly sequence N plus one.
minimumAssertions: Python validates the TypeScript file and manifest before destination publication.
Restored semantic root and continued global sequence are byte-identical.

cases.title: All Identity Equivalence
cases.objective: Both runtimes produce identical descriptor, schema, migration, baseline, request, result, manifest, and semantic roots.
minimumAssertions: Every portable byte carrier and domain-separated digest is compared exactly.
Only explicitly nonsemantic runtime metadata may differ.

cases.title: Alternating Runtime All Operations
cases.objective: TypeScript and Python alternate every sequence across all nine mutation operations and replay one identical final model.
minimumAssertions: Global sequence ownership alternates by runtime without gaps or partitions.
Both replay engines derive the same intermediate results and final physical root.

cases.title: Cross Runtime Request Byte Drift
cases.objective: A request carrier accepted by only one runtime is rejected as a conformance failure in both retained implementations.
minimumAssertions: Hostile numeric, Unicode, order, and boundary carriers are evaluated by both codecs.
No runtime-specific normalization produces a durable request row.

cases.title: Old Artifact New Schema Refusal
cases.objective: An installed artifact without schema-v2 support safely refuses a v2 file before any read-write mutation.
minimumAssertions: The old artifact returns the exact unsupported-version failure.
File, WAL, SHM, schema, baseline, operations, and sequence remain byte-identical.

cases.title: Installed NPM Lifecycle
cases.objective: A packed npm install creates or migrates, appends, reopens, exact-retries, audits, backs up, restores, and continues.
minimumAssertions: Every lifecycle call imports only from installed public exports and packaged assets.
Request, result, baseline, sequence, backup, and restored identities remain exact.

cases.title: Installed Wheel and Sdist Lifecycle
cases.objective: Isolated wheel and sdist installations each repeat the complete critical v2 provider lifecycle smoke.
minimumAssertions: Both artifacts contain byte-identical canonical migration resources and public codec exports.
Each isolated environment completes create or migrate through restore and continuation.

cases.title: Bounded Replay Characterization
cases.objective: Ten-thousand and one-hundred-thousand-operation replay records raw time, memory, and query plans without a throughput claim.
minimumAssertions: Raw samples, percentiles, record counts, database sizes, runtime versions, and plans are retained.
The report declares no release threshold, production throughput, or cross-language speed winner.

cases.title: Cancellation Hidden Commit
cases.objective: Python task cancellation may hide a committed sequence, but exact operation-ID retry returns it without allocating N plus one.
minimumAssertions: Cancellation is injected after commit and before acknowledgement at an exact barrier.
Retry after reopen returns stored result and leaves physical state and sequence count unchanged.

cases.title: Busy Full and IO Failure
cases.objective: Bounded BUSY, FULL, IOERR, and read-only failures retain sequence and state atomicity with safe error classes.
minimumAssertions: Each real or injected SQLite base code maps to its exact closed provider failure.
No failed transaction leaves a sequence gap, ledger-only row, mutation-only row, or active transaction.

cases.title: Path and Symlink Substitution
cases.objective: Migration, backup, and restore source or target substitution cannot redirect, alias, or overwrite trusted state.
minimumAssertions: Resolved source, destination, alias, hard-link, and symlink identities are checked before publication.
Every refusal preserves source and removes unpublished temporary targets.

cases.title: SQL Error Payload Leak
cases.objective: Raw SQL, expanded statements, paths, request and result bytes, and hostile sentinels never escape safe errors or reports.
minimumAssertions: Every structured and textual failure surface is scanned against all retained sentinels.
SQLite causes and statements remain unavailable outside the private adapter boundary.

cases.title: Event Cursor Tail Forgery
cases.objective: A coherent event snapshot tail hash and BLOB change without one matching immutable record fails semantic audit.
minimumAssertions: Cursor tenant, stream, tail sequence, and tail hash bind to an exact record row.
Rehashing the cursor snapshot cannot manufacture a valid immutable tail.

cases.title: Checkpoint Revision Forgery
cases.objective: A current checkpoint revision changed to a nonexistent or wrong retained revision fails semantic reconciliation.
minimumAssertions: Current checkpoint revision names its exact immutable put revision.
Changing a canonical current row and its summary together cannot bypass revision history.

cases.title: Backup Baseline Manifest Forgery
cases.objective: Changed baseline or sequence identity in a backup or sidecar manifest blocks restore and removes unpublished targets.
minimumAssertions: Source file bytes, semantic identities, and manifest domain hash are all verified before restore.
Every mismatch leaves the explicit destination and hidden publication paths absent.

cases.title: Migration Asset Byte Drift
cases.objective: One changed schema-v2 SQL, identity, manifest, fixture, or mirrored asset byte fails before migration execution.
minimumAssertions: Compiled trust anchors reject coordinated as well as single-copy replacement.
Source database application ID, user version, schema, and bytes remain unchanged.

cases.title: Evidence and Nonclaim Sentinel
cases.objective: Evidence validation rejects incomplete results, mutable references, missing cold gates, and unauthorized release or popularity claims.
minimumAssertions: Pending, skipped, expected-failure, waiver, mutable-ref, and missing-gate mutations all fail closed.
Release-ready, distributed-safety, production-throughput, Star-count, and popularity language are rejected.
